data.summary: Deprioritize. The paper by Heston and Sadka reports that stocks which did well in the same calendar month in earlier years tend to do well in that month again, and the tested version sorts stocks into deciles on average returns at annual lags 24, 36, 48, and 60 months. Our long-only, equal-weighted test on a 415-name survivor universe over 2015 to 2025 returned a net CAGR of 8.03% against 12.71% for the equal-weighted universe, with a Sharpe of 0.38 against 0.65. The Monte Carlo fund economics are also negative: the probability that the net present value is positive is 12%, and the median incremental fee present value is -$3.0M against the equal-weighted universe fund. The main reason for the recommendation is that the strategy trails its benchmark, the edge fails at 10 bps of costs, and the decile ranking runs opposite to the paper's expected direction.

sections.paper_proposes: Heston and Sadka (2006), "Seasonality in the Cross-Section of Stock Returns", argue that individual stocks persistently earn different returns in specific calendar months, so a stock that did well in a given calendar month in past years tends to do well in that same month again. The experiment selected for this run is the Table 2 Years 2-5 annual strategy. Each month, stocks are ranked into equal-count deciles on the average of their returns at annual lags 24, 36, 48, and 60 months, portfolios are equal-weighted and held one month, and the paper reports a winner-minus-loser spread of 67 basis points per month with a t-statistic of 5.35 over January 1965 to December 2002. The expected sign is that the favored (highest) decile earns more than the lowest.
sections.implemented_and_changed: We implemented the signal as the average of available annual-lag monthly returns at lags 24, 36, 48, and 60, ranked into 10 groups each month, equal-weighted, held one month, and rebalanced monthly. Execution uses the prior month's last close for the signal and the next month's first trading-day close for trades, with a cost of 10 bps. Four items were adapted: breakpoints are equal-count sorts over our eligible names rather than NYSE/AMEX stocks, the strategy is long-only so the paper's short leg is dropped, the universe is our 415-name S&P 500 survivor universe (19 names were excluded for missing Yahoo data), and the sample is 2015 to 2025 rather than 1965 to 2002. Five items were assumed because the paper is silent: no skip window, no price floor, a minimum of 2 available lags because the data snapshot starts in 2012 and the earliest formations have only lags 24 and 36, a history requirement of 252 days, and a formation-month minimum of 15 trading days. Eight details were left unresolved by the paper, including the return convention, delisting treatment, missing-return handling, and whether breakpoints use NYSE stocks only. The paper's text also conflicts with its own Table 2 on which decile is the winner, and we followed the table labeling. Limitations are stated plainly: survivor universe (which flatters returns), equal weighting, long-only, a sample that lies entirely after publication, zero yield on cash, and Yahoo adjusted-close return conventions.
sections.backtest_found: The long-only favored group earned a net CAGR of 8.03% (gross 10.29%) against 12.71% for the equal-weighted universe and a CAGR of 13.45% for SPY. Net Sharpe was 0.38 against 0.65 for the equal-weighted universe and 0.69 for SPY, and net max drawdown was -0.449151. The four-factor alpha t-statistic was -1.71 and the spanning alpha t-statistic was -2.27. Mean monthly turnover was 0.873087, which makes costs a large drag. At 0 bps the alpha t-statistic was -0.819607, and at 25 bps it was -3.02988. The ranked-group result goes the wrong way: group 10 earned a mean monthly return of 0.00812 while group 1 earned 0.011345, and the Spearman rho across groups was -0.71, not in the expected direction. The favored-minus-disfavored difference was -0.003226 per month with a Newey-West t-statistic of -1.0607. The edge over the equal-weighted universe fails at 10 bps and holds in 0 of 2 sub-periods.
sections.simulation_and_economics: The Monte Carlo resamples historical days in stationary blocks over 1000 paths, with a 5-year horizon and a seed of 20261028. The fund assumption is 2/20 with a 5% hard hurdle on a long-only equity strategy, which is an assumption and not an observed fee schedule, and incremental fees are measured against an equal-weighted universe fund charged the same schedule. The probability that net present value is positive is 12%, and the median incremental fee present value is -$3.0M. The strategy beat the equal-weighted fund in a fraction of 0.064 of paths and beat SPY in a fraction of 0.0 of paths. When the historical mean excess return over the equal-weighted fund is removed, the fraction of positive net present value paths is 0.495, which is what noise alone would give. Break-even AUM is not defined because expected incremental fees are not positive. The bootstrap cannot create regimes absent from the sample.
sections.interpretation_reliability: Extraction was a single run with a mean field agreement of 1.0, and evidence quotes were valid for 100% of the 16 fields checked, with no check-pass disagreements. Implementation reliability is rated amber because 5 fields were assumed and 4 were adapted. Agreement against the reference is weaker: the agreement rate was 0.461538 with 3 critical errors (signal formula, formation window, and favored group) and 4 minor errors. The reference describes the single-month lag 12 version of the paper and its 1.15 % per month headline, while the extraction selected the Years 2-5 annual variant with its 67 basis point headline, so part of the mismatch reflects a different choice of experiment rather than a misreading. The reference is preliminary, so this score should be read with care.
sections.next_steps: Deprioritize this strategy as tested. The test does not support the paper's result in a post-publication, long-only, survivor universe, and the economics are negative. If anyone revisits it, the useful steps are to resolve the preliminary reference and confirm which experiment variant is intended, test on a point-in-time universe that includes delisted names and a longer history so that all four annual lags are available, and consider the single-month lag 12 version. The long-only restriction and the roughly 87% monthly turnover would need to be addressed first for any of this to change the cost picture.
